series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator. The swap cache allocator is used by zswap writeback to allocate a folio that can be freed directly once writeback completes, without being on the LRU. This change does not introduce any functional changes and only modifies the internal implementation details of the swap cache allocator.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of drop-behind swap cache folios by freeing them immediately after writeback completion, rather than leaving them for reclaim to find later. This is done by adding two new functions: `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` and `swap_dropbehind_free_one_folio`, which are called when a synchronous-IO swap completes or an asynchronous block device completes writeback. The patch also updates the `remove_mapping` function to take additional parameters for tracking reclaim status and target memory cgroup. This change is necessary because synchronous-IO swaps can complete in the calling context, allowing the folio to be freed immediately, while asynchronous block devices require deferring the work to a workqueue that runs after writeback completion.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in zswap by dropping cold writeback folios via the swap dropbehind mechanism, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and keeping cold memory resident for shorter periods.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reintroduces a fixup mechanism to handle a specific scenario where a dio read operation sees a dirty destination page, but by the time it finishes reading, the page is clean due to btrfs writing it back. The fixup ensures that the dio read re-dirties the folio to prevent data corruption. This patch addresses an issue that was previously thought to be resolved with advances in preventing such re-dirtying, and reintroduces a mechanism that was first introduced in 2008.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] btrfs: use GFP_NOWAIT for tree block readahead

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] btrfs: use GFP_NOWAIT for tree block readahead

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs readahead mechanism to use GFP_NOWAIT instead of the default GFP_KERNEL allocation flag. This change is intended to prevent the readahead from blocking in direct reclaim, which can cause stalls and lock contention. The approach taken is to mark the extent buffer preallocation as supporting nowait allocation, allowing the system to fail the readahead if necessary rather than waiting for memory to become available.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] btrfs: enable unlocked NOFAIL retry for eb allocations

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] btrfs: enable unlocked NOFAIL retry for eb allocations

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch enables unlocked NOFAIL retry for extent buffer (eb) allocations in the Btrfs file system. It introduces a new struct, btrfs_eb_prealloc, to carry allocation information and signals when preallocation is required. If the allocation fails, it returns EAGAIN and allows the caller to retry with the eb, block device, and folios wired through in the prealloc struct. This approach aims to reduce reclaim stalls by allowing allocations that fail due to lack of memory to be retried without holding locks. However, two GFP_NOFS allocations remain under lock and cannot be preallocated.

The existing allocation pathways are refactored to use this new structure without any functional changes. Empty prealloc structs are wired in from callers, and several files have been modified as a result.

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 0/4] allocate extent_buffer GFP_NOFAIL with unlocked retry

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the Btrfs file system where allocations of extent_buffers are often made while holding btree locks, leading to contention and stalls. The patches introduce a mechanism to allocate these buffers with GFP_NOWAIT, then retry with GFP_NOFS | GFP_NOFAIL if necessary without holding any locks. This approach is analogous to how extent_buffers are read, which requires dropping locks. Although the series does not completely eliminate lock-holding allocations, it significantly reduces contention and stalls.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/21] iomap: split iomap_iter() logic into iomap_iter_next()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the iomap_iter() logic into a new helper function called iomap_iter_next(). The purpose of this change is to prepare for an upcoming modification to use an in-iterator model, where the ->iomap_next() callback will be able to directly call the iomap_iter_next() function. This allows for more flexibility and simplification of code. Additionally, two new macros are introduced to generate boilerplate wrapper functions for ->iomap_next(). The patch does not introduce any functional changes, but rather a code-level refactoring.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/21] iomap: decouple simple direct I/O reads from iomap_dio_rw
series_items.patch_summary: This patch decouples simple direct I/O reads from the iomap_dio_rw function to improve performance by allowing file systems to call into a new simple path explicitly, which can be inlined and optimized by the compiler. This change is necessary because the current implementation assumes that the iterator must be advanced at the end, but the direct I/O read fast path tries to avoid this. By splitting the simple path from iomap_dio_rw, file systems are required to only call the simple path for cases they can handle, and various checks for incompatible features can be dropped.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts the iomap code to use an iterator model, replacing the current begin/end pair of callbacks with a single next callback. This change allows for improved performance by enabling inlining and devirtualization of the iteration loop, as well as providing more flexibility for future callers to express custom logic in the IO path. The patches are broken down into 21 steps, including refactoring existing code, adding the new next callback, converting each filesystem, removing legacy paths, and updating documentation.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the iomap_iter() logic, moved it out into an inlined helper function called iomap_iter_next(), and provided macros to generate boilerplate ->iomap_next() wrapper functions. No functional change intended.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that the pending iomap_iter_next conversion creates performance issues for the new simple direct I/O read fast path, agreed to split the simple path from iomap_dio_rw and require file systems to call into it explicitly, and pass only a ->begin callback. This will allow dropping various checks for incompatible features while creating a requirement for the file system to only call the simple path for cases that it can handle.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about GFP_KERNEL allocation in non-blocking iocbs, agreed to switch to GFP_NOWAIT allocation instead.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the fallback path for filesystems that don't provide an ->iomap_next() callback, explaining that iomap_iter() will fall back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() path. The author's response suggests no immediate fix or revision needed.
review_comments.raw_body:
Have one ->iomap_next() callback instead of ->iomap_begin() and
->iomap_end(). ->iomap_next() finishes the previous mapping if needed,
and produces the next mapping.

Collapsing to a single callback lets a performance-critical caller
inline its iteration loop and pass its ->iomap_next() function as a
compile-time constant, so the compiler can devirtualize that callback
into a direct call instead of an indirect call through a function
pointer.

iomap_iter() uses ->iomap_next() when the filesystem provides that
callback and otherwise falls back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end()
path, so filesystems can be converted one at a time.

Suggested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Suggested-by: Matthew Wilcox (Oracle) <willy@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
---
 fs/iomap/iter.c       | 8 ++++++--
 include/linux/iomap.h | 9 +++++++++
 2 files changed, 15 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/fs/iomap/iter.c b/fs/iomap/iter.c
index 66ccb87441ab..e05574602946 100644
--- a/fs/iomap/iter.c
+++ b/fs/iomap/iter.c
@@ -107,8 +107,12 @@ int iomap_iter(struct iomap_iter *iter, const struct iomap_ops *ops)
 
 	trace_iomap_iter(iter, ops, _RET_IP_);
 
-	ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
-			ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+	if (ops->iomap_next)
+		ret = ops->iomap_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap);
+	else
+		ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
+				ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+
 	iter->status = 0;
 	if (ret > 0)
 		iomap_iter_done(iter);
diff --git a/include/linux/iomap.h b/include/linux/iomap.h
index 80832edc7ec2..d203d9fe0f89 100644
--- a/include/linux/iomap.h
+++ b/include/linux/iomap.h
@@ -231,9 +231,18 @@ typedef int (*iomap_iter_begin_fn)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos,
 typedef int (*iomap_iter_end_fn)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos, loff_t length,
 		ssize_t written, unsigned flags, struct iomap *iomap);
 
+/*
+ * Produce the next mapping (finishing the previous one if needed).
+ * Return 1 to continue iterating, 0 if the range is fully consumed, or a
+ * negative error on failure.
+ */
+typedef int (*iomap_iter_next_fn)(const struct iomap_iter *iter,
+		struct iomap *iomap, struct iomap *srcmap);
+
 struct iomap_ops {
 	iomap_iter_begin_fn iomap_begin;
 	iomap_iter_end_fn iomap_end;
+	iomap_iter_next_fn iomap_next;
 };
 
 /**

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: page_alloc: __GFP_FS lockdep annotation for direct compaction
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds lockdep annotations to the direct compaction function in the Linux kernel's page allocation code, specifically for __GFP_FS passing errors. This is done to prevent potential issues when compaction enters filesystem paths and to future-proof against unexpected behavior. The annotation is similar to one already present in direct reclaim code, which is often used in conjunction with compaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] mm: compaction: support non-movable compaction for pageblock requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the compaction algorithm in Linux by allowing non-movable direct compaction for pageblock requests, which is particularly useful in defrag_mode where whole blocks are produced and type mixing is not an issue.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Understood and agreed that the CMA interaction makes sense in this context. Provided a Reviewed-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 10:56:45AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> While trying to fix a reclaim storm in defrag_mode, I noticed that
> non-movable direct compaction is extremely inefficient.
> 
> When searching for space to evacuate, compaction only allows blocks of
> the same type as the incoming request. This is to prevent migratetype
> pollution, where a small non-movable request frees space in a movable
> block and provokes the allocator to fall back and pollute it.
> 
> This protection is reasonable on one hand, but the downside is that it
> makes non-movable direct compaction nearly useless: if we get the type
> annotations right, by definition there aren't any movable pages inside
> the non-movable blocks it is allowed to scan.
> 
> With defrag_mode, the goal is the production of whole blocks, which
> are essentially type neutral: __rmqueue_claim() will convert them
> wholesale on alloc. This makes type mixing and pollution a non-issue.
> 
> Fix the pollution gates to take the requested order into account, and
> allow whole-block requests to scan blocks of other types.
> 
> The only exception is CMA blocks. That type is sticky and these blocks
> cannot be claimed to other types. Continue to be strict with them, and
> allow only explicit ALLOC_CMA requests and kcompactd to evacuate them.
> 
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>

The CMA interaction took a second to grok but this makes sense.

Reviewed-by: Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] mm: page_alloc: move capture_control to the page allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the capture control from compaction's live compact control to the page allocator, allowing it to maintain its own copies of relevant information such as zone, migratetype, and allocation order. This change is necessary because defrag_mode promotes sub-block allocations to pageblock-order compaction, which can cause the allocation request order and compaction target order to differ. The patch also updates various functions in mm/compaction.c to pass the capture control through instead of a bare struct page pointer. No functional changes are introduced by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim storm in defrag_mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a 'reclaim storm' issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation system, specifically in defrag_mode. The problem occurs when non-movable requests spin in reclaim, causing excessive swapping and pressure spikes on certain workloads. To fix this, the patch sends non-movable requests into pageblock reclaim/compaction, allowing them to help move pages along and meet the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT bar. This approach is a temporary solution until a more comprehensive fix can be implemented to address scaling and concurrency limitations in compaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 04/12] mm/gup: let check_vma_flags() ignore selected VMA flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces an 'ignore_flags' argument to the check_vma_flags() function, allowing callers to selectively ignore certain VMA flags during GUP operations. The goal is to prepare for future changes in get_user_page_vma(), which will pass VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP to reach COWed pages.

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the interface being added and proposed replacing the mask with a single-purpose internal GUP flag, FOLL_PFNMAP_COW. Suggested an alternative implementation for the special-mapping gate.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 7/24/26 3:29 PM, Rik van Riel wrote:
> check_vma_flags() rejects a VMA whose flags gup cannot handle. A caller
> that wants to reach a COWed page in a VM_IO or VM_PFNMAP VMA, where that
> page does have a struct page, cannot express the exception and has to
> repeat the flag test itself.
> 
> Add an ignore_flags argument that check_vma_flags() clears from its local
> copy of vma->vm_flags before the flag checks. A caller can drop a single
> rejection this way while keeping every other check. All current callers
> pass 0.
>

> reach those COWed pages.
> 
> No functional change intended.

> Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-4.8
> Signed-off-by: Rik van Riel <riel@surriel.com>
> ---
>  mm/gup.c | 14 +++++++++++---
>  1 file changed, 11 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

> diff --git a/mm/gup.c b/mm/gup.c
> index 0692119b7904..dcece7b5253c 100644
> --- a/mm/gup.c
> +++ b/mm/gup.c
> @@ -1197,13 +1197,21 @@ static bool writable_file_mapping_allowed(struct vm_area_struct *vma,
>  	return !vma_needs_dirty_tracking(vma);
>  }

> -static int check_vma_flags(struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned long gup_flags)
> +static int check_vma_flags(struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned long gup_flags,
> +			   vm_flags_t ignore_flags)

All callers pass zero in this patch, so there is no behavior change yet.
The problem is the interface being added.

The same local vm_flags value is used for the VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP gate,
VM_WRITE, VM_SHADOW_STACK, VM_READ, VM_MAYREAD, and is_cow_mapping().

An arbitrary mask can therefore alter permission, shadow-stack, and COW
validation. For example, masking VM_SHARED changes the result of
is_cow_mapping(), while masking VM_SHADOW_STACK removes its write
rejection. Checks implemented through helpers still read the original
vma->vm_flags, so the meaning of ignore_flags also depends on how each
check happens to be implemented.

GUP flag, such as FOLL_PFNMAP_COW, and apply it only to the
special-mapping gate:

	if (vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP) &&
	    (!(gup_flags & FOLL_PFNMAP_COW) ||
	     !(vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP)))
		return -EFAULT;

keeping VM_IO-only mappings and every other VMA check unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 05/12] mm/gup: add get_user_page_vma() to fault in a page under a held lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called get_user_page_vma() to the Linux kernel's mm/gup.c file. It is designed to fault in a single page under a held lock, either the mmap lock or the per-VMA lock. The function simplifies __get_user_pages() by walking the page tables with follow_page_mask(), faults in missing pages with faultin_page(), and returns the page with a reference still held by the caller. It also includes checks for VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP VMA exceptions, userfaultfd VMA handling, and error cases where the lock is released and -EAGAIN is returned.

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer John Hubbard noted that the get_user_page_vma() function does not handle the case where a page is already mapped in the VMA's page tables, and requested that the function check for this condition before attempting to fault in the page.

The reviewer pointed out a difference in behavior between VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP VMA types, noting that VM_IO only indicates that MM callers should not inspect the mapped pages due to side effects, whereas VM_PFNMAP identifies mappings whose COWed pages should be returned. The reviewer suggested testing for VM_PFNMAP specifically instead of treating both as exceptions.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 7/24/26 3:29 PM, Rik van Riel wrote:
...

---

This treats VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP as the same exception, but they have
different meanings. VM_IO tells MM callers not to inspect the mapped
pages because accesses can have side effects. It does not imply that
the VMA contains raw PFNs!

For example, sg_mmap() creates a VM_IO-only VMA whose fault handler
installs ordinary pages from the SCSI reserve buffer. If such a page is
already present, follow_page_mask() returns it before the pfnmap test
below is reached. Patch 6 then lets /proc/PID/mem and ptrace copy that
page directly, even though sg provides no ->access callback and the
operation fails today. Writes can also modify the buffer when the
mapping is writable. Existing ptrace authorization still applies, so
this is not a privilege bypass, but it removes the VM_IO exclusion for
a driver that did not opt in through ->access.

An untouched page in the same VMA still fails because pfnmap is also
true for VM_IO and this function refuses to fault it. The result
therefore depends on whether the target previously touched the page.
The required exception is narrower. A remap_pfn_range() VMA has both
VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP, but VM_PFNMAP is what identifies the mapping whose
COWed page should be returned. 

So if you use the FOLL_PFNMAP_COW flag suggested on patch 4, and test
only VM_PFNMAP here:

	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags);
	if (ret)
		goto fail;
	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP;

Patch 6 can set FOLL_PFNMAP_COW for __access_remote_vm().
check_vma_flags() then permits VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP for that caller while
continuing to reject VM_IO-only mappings. vm_normal_page() supplies the
remaining distinction: it returns the COWed normal page and rejects the
raw PFN.

Something like that.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 06/12] mm: use per-VMA lock in __access_remote_vm() for single-VMA accesses
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the __access_remote_vm() function to use a per-VMA lock when accessing memory from a remote process, but falls back to the mmap_lock if the access crosses VMA boundaries or cannot be completed under the per-VMA lock. The patch also introduces new functions for handling remote accesses and page table walks, including remote_access_lock(), remote_access_unlock(), and get_user_page_vma(). These changes aim to reduce contention between readers and writers on large machines running multi-threaded applications, improving performance in scenarios like reading /proc/PID/cmdline or /proc/PID/mem.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 07/12] mm: read remote strings under the per-VMA lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the __copy_remote_vm_str() function to read remote strings under a per-VMA lock instead of the mmap read lock, reducing contention and improving performance. The new implementation uses the existing remote_vm_walk() function with a copy_vm_str() action that copies each page and stops at the NUL character. If the string is too long, it falls back to the original mmap lock path. This change aims to improve the efficiency of reading strings from other processes' memory spaces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 08/12] selftests/mm: cover /proc/pid/mem access to VM_PFNMAP memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two tests to the selftests/mm/pfnmap.c file to cover reading VM_PFNMAP memory through /proc/pid/mem. The first test, procmem_cow_read, maps a private and writable file, writes to a copy-on-write (COW) page, and then reads it back through /proc/self/mem. Without the struct-page path in get_user_page_vma(), this read would fall back to generic_access_phys() and ioremap of a COWed RAM page is rejected. The second test, procmem_pfn_read, reads a raw PFN back through ->access(). This patch exercises __access_remote_vm() two ways: through the struct-page path in get_user_page_vma() and through vma->vm_ops->access(), which ioremaps the PFN.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 09/12] mm/gup: build get_user_page_lookup_vma() on get_user_page_vma()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the `get_user_page_lookup_vma()` function to reuse the existing `get_user_page_vma()` helper, eliminating duplicated code and improving performance. The new implementation holds the mmap lock throughout the call, ensuring that the VMA remains valid even in case of a fault. It also preserves the foreign-access permission check and accessed-bit behavior. The patch removes the old implementation and adds an assertion to ensure that the caller holds the mmap lock.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 10/12] mm/gup: pass an end address to follow_page_mask() and return a page count
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the mm/gup module to return the number of contiguous pages covered by a page, rather than a bitmask representing the enclosing huge page. The function now takes an additional 'end' argument that bounds how far the walk looks, allowing for more efficient handling of large folios and preventing unnecessary scanning. This change is intended to facilitate batching PTE-mapped large folios in a later patch without introducing functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 11/12] mm/gup: batch contiguous PTE-mapped large folios in follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of PTE-mapped large folios in follow_page_mask() by batching contiguous pages together, reducing the number of page table walks required for these mappings. The optimization is based on the observation that huge PMD and PUD paths already return the whole mapping in one step, and applies a similar approach to the PTE case. The patch also ensures that per-PTE guarantees are maintained for the head page.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 12/12] selftests/mm: add a slow-GUP content and COW test for mTHP
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test, mthp_gup_cow_test, to the Linux kernel selftests suite. The test checks that the slow get_user_pages() path correctly handles large folios (mTHP) and copy-on-write (COW) operations. It does this by pinning a region of memory on the slow path, writing a distinct pattern to each page, and then verifying that the kernel copies back the correct contents from the pinned pages after a COW operation. patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch renames the function get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma() to improve namespace clarity and prepare for a new variant of this function that takes a VMA as an argument. The rename is done in multiple files, including arch-specific code and include files. This change does not introduce any functional changes.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about check_vma_flags() rejecting VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP VMA flags, which prevents reaching COWed pages in these mappings. The author added an ignore_flags argument to check_vma_flags(), allowing callers to drop specific rejections while keeping others. This change prepares for get_user_page_vma(), which will pass VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP to reach those COWed pages.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed concerns about contention on large multi-threaded workloads between readers and writers of mmap() or munmap(), which stall readers like /proc/PID/cmdline, /proc/PID/environ, or /proc/PID/mem. The author proposed using the per-VMA lock to access a remote process's memory when the access fits in one VMA, adding an unlocked variant of untagged_addr_remote() and annotating reads with READ_ONCE() and writes with WRITE_ONCE() for KCSAN-clean accesses.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about contention on mmap_read_lock() in __access_remote_vm(), explaining that using per-VMA lock would avoid this issue and provide a modest speedup. The author confirmed they will use the per-VMA lock when an access fits within one VMA, but fall back to the mmap lock for multi-VMA accesses or other cases.
review_comments.raw_body:
__access_remote_vm() holds mmap_read_lock() for the whole transfer. On
large machines, with large multi-threaded applications, the mmap_lock
is often contended, leading to things like reads of /proc/PID/cmdline
stalling.

This results in system monitoring tools getting stuck, right when
system information would be the most helpful.

That problem can be avoided by having __access_remote_vm() access
user memory under the per-VMA lock. The old code also looks up
the VMA for every page accessed, and walks the page tables for
every page inside a large folio. Cleaning that up speeds things
up nicely.

Using code that does not include its own lock dance, and does not
look up the VMA twice results in a modest speedup.

	read size   baseline    per-VMA     throughput
	8 B          201.7 ns    170.6 ns    ~15% faster
	4 KB         495 ns      442 ns      +12% (8266 -> 9265 MB/s)
	64 KB       4115 ns     3355 ns      +23% (15927 -> 19536 MB/s)
	1 MB       75902 ns    63641 ns      +19% (13815 -> 16477 MB/s)

The multi-threaded reader-versus-writer contention that motivates the lock
is not measured.

The rest of the series builds on this to batch per-VMA GUP. Patches 9-12
have follow_page_mask() report a contiguous PTE-mapped run of a large
folio, so the slow pin_user_pages() path walks it once instead of per page.
Other paths that walk a range benefit too.

That batching pays off on PTE-mapped mTHP. With mm/gup_test.c
(PIN_LONGTERM_BENCHMARK, the slow pin_user_pages() path) on a 256 MB
MADV_HUGEPAGE region in a 4 CPU VM, median get time over 16 iterations:

	gup_test -L -m 256 -n 65536 -r 16 -t
	                      before      after
	64 kB mTHP            3140 us      412 us   (7.6x)
	2 MB THP (control)      78 us       76 us
	4 kB base (control)   3010 us     3042 us

The PMD-mapped 2 MB THP already returns in one step, so only the PTE-mapped
large folio case improves.

Reaching a page under the per-VMA lock means looking up the VMA first,
which needs to untag the remote address without the mmap lock. The untag
masks (x86 LAM, riscv pointer masking) change only while the target is
single-threaded, so a remote reader races at most one such change.

Those masks are already read locklessly elsewhere, so patches 1 and 2 add
untagged_addr_remote_unlocked() helpers with READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE()
annotations. A stale read sees the old or new mask, never a torn value, and
the remote untag is best-effort.

With the VMA in hand we need one page from it under the lock the caller
already holds. get_user_pages_remote() does not fit: it hard codes the mmap
lock and re-derives the VMA internally.

Rather than reimplement GUP in yet another caller, this version follows
David Hildenbrand's v2 guidance: start from a proper GUP interface that
takes a locked VMA, not an mm, and decide which faults can resolve under
the VMA lock.

Patch 3 renames get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma() to
free the name. Patch 5 adds get_user_page_vma(): a simplified
__get_user_pages() that walks the tables with follow_page_mask(), faults a
missing page in with faultin_page(), and returns it with a reference and
the caller's lock still held.

Like __get_user_pages() it runs check_vma_flags(), so callers need not
pre-check the VMA.

A VM_IO or VM_PFNMAP VMA is the exception: a COWed page with a struct page
is returned normally, while a raw PFN yields -EFAULT so the caller can
reach vma->vm_ops->access(). The caller sets FOLL_VMA_LOCK when it holds
the per-VMA lock, which reaches the fault code as FAULT_FLAG_VMA_LOCK.

Anything the per-VMA lock cannot finish releases the lock and returns
-EAGAIN, so the caller retries under the mmap lock: a dropped fault, a
userfaultfd VMA (which assumes current is the faulting task), a hard error,
or ->access() memory. faultin_page() reports the retry the same way for
both lock types.

__access_remote_vm() then uses the per-VMA lock when an access fits within
one VMA, and falls back to the mmap lock for multi-VMA accesses, stack
expansion, or an -EAGAIN from get_user_page_vma().

Walking page tables under only the per-VMA lock is safe against both page
table freeing and THP collapse. munmap() frees a VMA's page tables under
the VMA write lock that our read lock excludes, so they cannot be torn down
under the walk.

THP collapse needs neither lock: it retracts a PTE page under the page
table lock and frees it by RCU.

follow_page_pte() takes that same lock through pte_offset_map_lock() and
rechecks the pmd, so it either walks an intact table or sees the collapsed
pmd and faults the page in, while RCU keeps the retracted page valid.

A COWed page in a VM_PFNMAP mapping was previously unreachable through
/proc/pid/mem because generic_access_phys() rejects ioremaps of RAM. With
get_user_page_vma() returning the struct page directly, that read now
succeeds, which the new selftests cover along with the raw PFN path.

Thanks to Suren for pointing out the need, to David for pushing me
to just rework the whole area, to Usama for reviewing the arch patches,
and Lorenzo for the changelog and cover letter cleanups.

There is a lot more work that could be done in this area, but the
patch series is big enough. More changes can come in follow up work.

review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about contention on the mmap lock in __access_remote_vm() due to large multi-threaded workloads, and has proposed adding an unlocked variant of untagged_addr_remote() to resolve this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
__access_remote_vm() reads another task's memory under the mmap lock. That
lock is contended on large multi-threaded workloads, where an mmap() or
munmap() stalls readers like /proc/PID/cmdline or process_vm_readv() even
though the target memory is resident and reachable under the per-VMA lock.

Reaching it under the per-VMA lock means looking up the VMA first, which
requires untagging the remote address without the mmap lock. riscv's
untagged_addr_remote() asserts that lock and has no unlocked variant; the
generic untagged_addr_remote_unlocked() falls back to untagged_addr(),
which masks against current->mm, not the target mm.

Add untagged_addr_remote_unlocked(), which masks @addr against the target
mm without asserting the lock, and redefine untagged_addr_remote() on top
of it so it keeps the assertion.

The mask width is mm->context.pmlen, written while a program is single
threaded, and frozen with MM_CONTEXT_LOCK_PMLEN once it spawns a second
thread.

That read need not be stable: pmlen is already read locklessly by
untagged_addr() and mm_untag_mask(), and a remote untag is best-effort.
Annotate the lockless reads with READ_ONCE() and the writes with
WRITE_ONCE(), so a reader sees one whole value and the accesses are
KCSAN-clean.

> +			   vm_flags_t ignore_flags)

All callers pass zero in this patch, so there is no behavior change yet.
The problem is the interface being added.

The same local vm_flags value is used for the VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP gate,
VM_WRITE, VM_SHADOW_STACK, VM_READ, VM_MAYREAD, and is_cow_mapping().

An arbitrary mask can therefore alter permission, shadow-stack, and COW
validation. For example, masking VM_SHARED changes the result of
is_cow_mapping(), while masking VM_SHADOW_STACK removes its write
rejection. Checks implemented through helpers still read the original
vma->vm_flags, so the meaning of ignore_flags also depends on how each
check happens to be implemented.

Perhaps it is best to replace the mask with a single-purpose internal
GUP flag, such as FOLL_PFNMAP_COW, and apply it only to the
special-mapping gate:

	if (vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP) &&
	    (!(gup_flags & FOLL_PFNMAP_COW) ||
	     !(vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP)))
		return -EFAULT;

This permits the later caller to examine a VM_PFNMAP mapping while
keeping VM_IO-only mappings and every other VMA check unchanged.



thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

On 7/24/26 3:29 PM, Rik van Riel wrote:
...
> +struct page *get_user_page_vma(struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned long addr,
...
> +	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags, VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP);
> +	if (ret)
> +		goto fail;
> +	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP);

This treats VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP as the same exception, but they have
different meanings. VM_IO tells MM callers not to inspect the mapped
pages because accesses can have side effects. It does not imply that
the VMA contains raw PFNs!

For example, sg_mmap() creates a VM_IO-only VMA whose fault handler
installs ordinary pages from the SCSI reserve buffer. If such a page is
already present, follow_page_mask() returns it before the pfnmap test
below is reached. Patch 6 then lets /proc/PID/mem and ptrace copy that
page directly, even though sg provides no ->access callback and the
operation fails today. Writes can also modify the buffer when the
mapping is writable. Existing ptrace authorization still applies, so
this is not a privilege bypass, but it removes the VM_IO exclusion for
a driver that did not opt in through ->access.

An untouched page in the same VMA still fails because pfnmap is also
true for VM_IO and this function refuses to fault it. The result
therefore depends on whether the target previously touched the page.
The required exception is narrower. A remap_pfn_range() VMA has both
VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP, but VM_PFNMAP is what identifies the mapping whose
COWed page should be returned. 

So if you use the FOLL_PFNMAP_COW flag suggested on patch 4, and test
only VM_PFNMAP here:

	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags);
	if (ret)
		goto fail;
	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP;

Patch 6 can set FOLL_PFNMAP_COW for __access_remote_vm().
check_vma_flags() then permits VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP for that caller while
continuing to reject VM_IO-only mappings. vm_normal_page() supplies the
remaining distinction: it returns the COWed normal page and rejects the
raw PFN.

Something like that.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

> where the reaper was blocked and the memcg never fell below the limit.

> entering out_of_memory and the storm is gone.
> 
> With the following suggestion, the threads of dying tasks stop entering
> out_of_memory but the exit time doubled as each thread has to decompress the
> page from zswap.
> 
> 	if (tsk_is_oom_victim(current))
> 		goto force;
> 
> I also tested by replacing goto force with goto nomem and the exit time halved
> i.e. ~20 seconds. Looking deeper it seems like each thread is still going
> through the reclaim loops.
> 
> Just for testing purpose I moved this check along with goto nomem just before
> the reclaim fuction i.e. try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages() and the exit time falls
> below 1 second. I think what we need is to detect early that the cgroup is
> unreclaimable and the threads of exiting/reaped process should just return with
> enomem.

Do you mean, something like this?
--- 
diff --git a/mm/memcontrol.c b/mm/memcontrol.c
index 6dc4888a90f3..66f1eebf8c22 100644
--- a/mm/memcontrol.c
+++ b/mm/memcontrol.c
@@ -2648,6 +2648,18 @@ static int try_charge_memcg(struct mem_cgroup *memcg, gfp_t gfp_mask,
 	if (!gfpflags_allow_blocking(gfp_mask))
 		goto nomem;
 
+	/*
+	 * OOM victim still needs to charge memory to exit. OOM reaper should
+	 * help but it might fail on mmap_lock contention. If the victim is a
+	 * large thread group then all exiting threads might compete on oom_lock
+	 * just to learn that there is nothing really killable anymore. Bail
+	 * out early and fail the charge to expedite their exit. They are
+	 * considered fully reclaimed by the oom reaper and they shouldn't contribute
+	 * further charges.
+	 */
+	if (tsk_is_oom_victim(current) && mm_flags_test(current->signal->oom_mm))
+		goto nomem;
+
 	__memcg_memory_event(mem_over_limit, MEMCG_MAX, allow_spinning);
 	raised_max_event = true;

Michal Hocko

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: The patch addresses a memory congestion control group (memcg) Out-Of-Memory (OOM) issue caused by robust futexes on exit, which leads to a storm of OOM events. The problem occurs when the kernel fails to properly clean up resources allocated for futexes during process exit. This patch attempts to resolve the issue by improving the handling of futex cleanup and resource deallocation.

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the patch's performance impact, specifically the exit time of dying tasks. They tested two approaches: one that uses goto force and another that uses goto nomem, finding that the latter reduces exit time by half. The author suggests detecting early that the cgroup is unreclaimable to avoid unnecessary reclaim loops.
review_comments.raw_body:
I have some results with the reproducer I (AI) wrote.

Setup: 20k threads, each with its robust_list head on its own page in a
large anon region pushed into a zswap pool (writeback off, so it's
unreclaimable and pins the memcg at the limit). On the OOM-group-kill
every thread faults that page in futex_cleanup() -> do_swap_page() ->
swapin charge -> memcg OOM. A separate thread holds mmap_lock for write
in a loop so the oom_reaper can't reap the pool -- matching the host,
where the reaper was blocked and the memcg never fell below the limit.

I tested on next-20260726 as baseline and then tested your suggestion over it.
For baseline ~48k no-victim OOM invocations serialized on oom_lock; ~40s to
drain the 20k threads in a VM (hours on the host, where each invocation
was a dump_header over netconsole). With the patch the dying tasks stop
entering out_of_memory and the storm is gone.

With the following suggestion, the threads of dying tasks stop entering
out_of_memory but the exit time doubled as each thread has to decompress the
page from zswap.

	if (tsk_is_oom_victim(current))
		goto force;

I also tested by replacing goto force with goto nomem and the exit time halved
i.e. ~20 seconds. Looking deeper it seems like each thread is still going
through the reclaim loops.

Just for testing purpose I moved this check along with goto nomem just before
the reclaim fuction i.e. try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages() and the exit time falls
below 1 second. I think what we need is to detect early that the cgroup is
unreclaimable and the threads of exiting/reaped process should just return with
enomem.
